title: When NOT to Use Design Patterns

content.title: When NOT to Use Design Patterns

blocks.content: Every engineer who has just learned design patterns goes through the same phase. Suddenly every class needs a factory, every branch needs a strategy, and every object creation needs a builder.

This is not a character flaw. It is what happens when a new tool feels powerful and you want to use it everywhere. The problem is that patterns are supposed to solve recurring structural problems, not decorate code that was already fine.
A pattern applied where it is not needed does not make code more professional. It makes it harder to read, harder to change, and harder for the next engineer to trust.
This lesson is about the other half of learning patterns: knowing when to leave them on the shelf.
A design pattern that solves no real problem is not architecture, it is just extra code standing between you and the answer.
1. The Pattern Happy Phase
Once you can name a pattern, you start seeing it everywhere, whether it belongs there or not.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499287605-909496355.png
blocks.alt: Decision flow contrasting applying a pattern to every problem versus checking the fit first

blocks.content: Real World Analogy
Imagine a carpenter who just learned to use a router. Suddenly every joint in every project gets routed, even the ones a simple butt joint would have handled fine.
The tool is not wrong. The judgment about when to reach for it is what is missing.
How This Shows Up In Code
blocks.text: How This Shows Up In Code

blocks.content: A junior to mid level engineer reads about the Strategy pattern on Monday. By Friday, every if or switch statement in the codebase has been rewritten as a family of strategy classes.
None of those branches were ever going to grow past two or three cases. The refactor added files, added indirection, and added nothing else.

blocks.title: Why this happens
blocks.content: Patterns are memorable and satisfying to apply. Restraint is not memorable. That asymmetry is why overuse is so common early in a career.
A Related Trap: Prestige Over Judgment
blocks.text: A Related Trap: Prestige Over Judgment

blocks.content: Some engineers reach for a pattern because it signals seniority, not because the problem needs it. A pull request full of interfaces and factories can look impressive to a less experienced reviewer.
That impression fades fast once someone has to actually extend or debug the code. Prestige is not a design goal, and code should never be optimized for how clever it looks in a diff.
2. What A Pattern Is Actually Paying For
blocks.text: 2. What A Pattern Is Actually Paying For

blocks.content: Every pattern is a trade. You give up some directness and simplicity, and in exchange you are supposed to get flexibility, testability, or clarity that you will actually use.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499290645-448575929.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing the cost paid now against the benefit promised later, and whether that benefit ever gets used

blocks.content: The Trade In Plain Terms

["You add an interface and one or more implementing classes.","You add a layer of indirection between the caller and the real work.","You add new vocabulary a reader has to learn before the code makes sense.","In exchange, you are supposed to gain the ability to swap, extend, or test something independently."]
items: You add an interface and one or more implementing classes.
You add a layer of indirection between the caller and the real work.
You add new vocabulary a reader has to learn before the code makes sense.
In exchange, you are supposed to gain the ability to swap, extend, or test something independently.

blocks.content: If that exchange does not happen, if nothing ever gets swapped, extended, or tested independently, you paid the cost and got nothing back.
The Test That Matters
Ask what this pattern lets you do that a plain function or a plain if statement could not. If the honest answer is nothing, the pattern is decoration.
A Simple Mental Model
Think of every pattern as a loan. You are borrowing readability today against a promise of flexibility later.
A loan you never draw on is still debt. The interest is paid by every engineer who has to read the extra layer before they can trust what the code does.
3. Example: Strategy For Two Options That Will Never Change
blocks.text: 3. Example: Strategy For Two Options That Will Never Change

blocks.content: The Strategy pattern earns its keep when the set of behaviors is genuinely open ended, chosen at runtime, and likely to grow.
A Pattern That Adds Nothing
Consider a shipping cost calculator that only ever has two modes, standard and express. Nobody on the roadmap is planning a third mode.
Wrapping that in a ShippingStrategy interface with StandardShippingStrategy and ExpressShippingStrategy classes plus a context object turns a two line if statement into five files.
The Direct Version Doing The Same Job
blocks.text: The Direct Version Doing The Same Job

blocks.content: A single function with a plain conditional says exactly the same thing in a fraction of the lines, and a new engineer understands it in seconds.
If a third or fourth shipping mode shows up later, that is the moment to consider Strategy, not before it.
4. Example: Factory For A Class With One Constructor
blocks.text: 4. Example: Factory For A Class With One Constructor

blocks.content: A Factory pattern earns its keep when creating an object is genuinely complicated, when the concrete type depends on runtime input, or when construction needs to be hidden from callers.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499292145-714425823.png
blocks.alt: Diagram comparing a class wrapped in an unnecessary factory against calling its constructor directly

blocks.content: A Pattern That Adds Nothing
A class with a single straightforward constructor does not need a factory. Wrapping it in one just renames "new" and adds a hop.
The Direct Version Doing The Same Job
blocks.text: The Direct Version Doing The Same Job

blocks.content: Calling the constructor directly is exactly as safe and exactly as readable, minus one class and one indirection hop.
A factory becomes worth it once construction involves choosing between several concrete types, reading configuration, or hiding a complex build sequence. A single constructor never needed one.

The same logic applies to Abstract Factory, Builder, and every other creational pattern. The question is always whether construction itself is the hard part of the problem, not whether a pattern exists that could technically wrap it.
5. Seeing The Difference
The diagram below lines up a plain function call next to a fully patterned version of the same notification feature. Both send a single email. Only one of them needs to exist.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494343451-34660400.png
blocks.alt: Direct solution next to an unnecessarily pattern heavy solution for the same task

blocks.content: Notice that the pattern heavy side has more boxes and more arrows for identical behavior. Every extra box is something a future reader has to hold in their head before they can trust the code.
6. The Real Cost Of Premature Pattern Application
blocks.text: 6. The Real Cost Of Premature Pattern Application

blocks.content: The cost of an unnecessary pattern rarely shows up as a bug. It shows up as friction that accumulates quietly over months.
Harder To Read
A reader has to trace through an interface, an implementation, and a context object to find behavior that used to be one function away.
Harder To Onboard
New engineers spend their first weeks learning the shape of your abstractions instead of learning the actual business problem the code solves.
More Moving Parts
Every extra class is one more place a bug can hide, one more file to keep in sync, and one more thing that has to be updated when requirements shift.
False Sense Of Flexibility
Teams often believe a pattern has made their code future proof, then discover the actual future requirement does not fit the abstraction they built and has to be worked around anyway.

{"headers":["Cost","What It Looks Like In Practice"],"rows":[["Reading tax","Following one behavior across three or four files instead of one"],["Onboarding tax","New hires learn your abstractions before they learn the domain"],["Change tax","A small requirement tweak now touches an interface and every implementer"],["Trust tax","Reviewers assume the pattern must be load bearing and hesitate to simplify it"]]}
Compounding Over Time
None of these costs is dramatic on its own. A single unnecessary factory or strategy rarely sinks a project by itself.
The damage comes from compounding. A codebase with dozens of small, unearned abstractions becomes slow to work in long before anyone can point to a single cause.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499293601-456866585.png
blocks.alt: Diagram showing reading, onboarding, change, and trust costs compounding into a codebase that is slow to work in

blocks.content: 7. Telling A Real Problem From A Decorated One
blocks.text: 7. Telling A Real Problem From A Decorated One

blocks.content: Before reaching for a pattern, ask what would actually break or get harder without it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499295335-439868891.png
blocks.alt: Decision flow showing whether to keep simple direct code or let the pattern earn its place

blocks.content: Questions Worth Asking

["Will there realistically be more than two or three variants of this behavior within the next year, not in theory but on the actual roadmap?","Does this object get created in more than one place, with different concrete types chosen at runtime?","Is construction genuinely complex, involving multiple steps, optional pieces, or validation that would otherwise be duplicated?","Will a test need to substitute a fake implementation for this specific piece and nothing else?","Does removing the pattern and inlining the logic make the code harder to follow, not easier?"]
items: Will there realistically be more than two or three variants of this behavior within the next year, not in theory but on the actual roadmap?
Does this object get created in more than one place, with different concrete types chosen at runtime?
Is construction genuinely complex, involving multiple steps, optional pieces, or validation that would otherwise be duplicated?
Will a test need to substitute a fake implementation for this specific piece and nothing else?
Does removing the pattern and inlining the logic make the code harder to follow, not easier?

blocks.content: If most of the honest answers are no, the code you have right now, before any pattern was added, is probably the right amount of structure.
A Useful Reversal
Instead of asking "which pattern fits this problem," try writing the simplest version first. Only reach for a pattern when the simple version visibly strains under real, current requirements.

blocks.title: The reversal in one line
blocks.content: Let the pain justify the pattern. Do not let the pattern go looking for pain to justify itself.
This reversal also makes code review easier. A pull request that adds a pattern alongside the requirement that forced it is far easier to trust than one that adds a pattern speculatively.
8. Signs You Are Overapplying A Pattern
blocks.text: 8. Signs You Are Overapplying A Pattern

blocks.content: What This Looks Like Day To Day
blocks.text: What This Looks Like Day To Day

blocks.content: These signals show up during code review and during day to day maintenance, often before anyone names the actual problem.

["You can describe the pattern in the code, but nobody can describe the problem it was solving.","There is exactly one implementation of an interface that was meant to support many.","A reviewer asks \"why is this a class\" and the honest answer is \"it felt more proper.\"","Adding a genuinely new case still requires touching three files instead of one, because the abstraction guessed the wrong axis of change.","Removing the pattern and inlining the code makes the diff smaller and the behavior identical."]
items: You can describe the pattern in the code, but nobody can describe the problem it was solving.
There is exactly one implementation of an interface that was meant to support many.
A reviewer asks "why is this a class" and the honest answer is "it felt more proper."
Adding a genuinely new case still requires touching three files instead of one, because the abstraction guessed the wrong axis of change.
Removing the pattern and inlining the code makes the diff smaller and the behavior identical.

blocks.title: A Quick Gut Check
blocks.text: Delete the interface in your head and imagine calling the concrete class directly. If nothing about the call site, the tests, or the readability gets worse, the interface was not paying rent.

blocks.content: 9. A Grounded Checklist Before Reaching For A Pattern
blocks.text: 9. A Grounded Checklist Before Reaching For A Pattern

blocks.content: Use this checklist as a short pause before committing to a pattern, not as a ritual to justify one you already decided to use.

["Name the concrete pain the pattern removes, in one sentence, without naming the pattern itself.","Confirm there are at least two real variants today, or a near certain third one on the roadmap.","Confirm the abstraction lines up with the axis that actually changes, not just any axis that could theoretically change.","Estimate the number of new files and interfaces the pattern introduces, and ask if that count is proportional to the problem.","Check whether a plain function, a plain conditional, or a plain constructor call would read just as clearly.","Ask a teammate unfamiliar with the change to read both versions and say which one they would rather maintain."]
items: Name the concrete pain the pattern removes, in one sentence, without naming the pattern itself.
Confirm there are at least two real variants today, or a near certain third one on the roadmap.
Confirm the abstraction lines up with the axis that actually changes, not just any axis that could theoretically change.
Estimate the number of new files and interfaces the pattern introduces, and ask if that count is proportional to the problem.
Check whether a plain function, a plain conditional, or a plain constructor call would read just as clearly.
Ask a teammate unfamiliar with the change to read both versions and say which one they would rather maintain.

blocks.content: {"pros":["Patterns applied where they fit make future variation cheap and predictable.","A shared vocabulary of patterns speeds up communication among engineers who already know them.","The right pattern in the right place reduces duplicated logic."],"cons":["Patterns applied where they do not fit add files and indirection with no payoff.","Unused flexibility is a maintenance cost that never gets cashed in.","Overapplied patterns slow down onboarding and code review."]}
Revisit The Decision Later
A pattern that earned its place a year ago can stop earning it. Requirements shrink, variants get retired, and an abstraction that once tracked three real cases can end up tracking one.

blocks.title: Treat this as ongoing
blocks.content: Reviewing whether an old pattern still earns its complexity deserves the same attention as deciding whether to add a new one.
10. Closing Thoughts
Design patterns are answers to problems that show up repeatedly across codebases. They are not a checklist to complete or a signal of seniority.

The engineers who use patterns well are not the ones who apply the most of them. They are the ones who can point at the exact pain a pattern removes, and who are just as comfortable deleting a pattern that stopped earning its place.
Practical Takeaway
Write the direct, boring version first. Reach for a pattern only when that direct version visibly struggles under real requirements, not hypothetical ones.
Simple code that does the job is not a missed opportunity for architecture. It is the architecture, until the day it genuinely is not enough.
